---
title: "Leverage and Leave-One-Out Diagnostics"
description: "Find influential observations in regressions with high-dimensional fixed effects."
categories: [inference, fixed effects, performance]
jupyter: python3
---

Leverage measures how strongly each observation influences its own fitted
value. PyFixest can calculate it without constructing the full dummy-variable
matrix, even when a regression absorbs high-dimensional fixed effects.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pyfixest as pf

data = pf.get_data()
fit = pf.feols("Y ~ X1 + X2 | f1 + f2", data)

leverage = fit.hatvalues(
    reps=200,
    rng=np.random.default_rng(42),
)
leverage[:5]
```

## Exact and randomized calculations

`method="auto"`, the default, uses an exact calculation for regressions with
zero or one fixed effect. With two or more fixed effects it uses a
Johnson--Lindenstrauss approximation (JLA) with Rademacher probes, following
[Kline, Saggio, and Sølvsten (2020)](https://doi.org/10.3982/ECTA16410).

JLA repeatedly projects random vectors using the same demeaner configured for
estimation. The vectors are processed in bounded-memory batches, so neither the
fixed-effect dummy matrix nor an observations-by-repetitions matrix is stored.
Increasing `reps` improves precision at a proportional runtime cost.

For very large, sparse multiway fixed effects, fit with the `within` LSMR
backend. Its reusable preconditioner is particularly effective for the repeated
right-hand sides required by JLA:

```{python}
large_fit = pf.feols(
    "Y ~ X1 + X2 | f1 + f2",
    data,
    demeaner=pf.LsmrDemeaner(),
)
large_fit.hatvalues(reps=200, rng=np.random.default_rng(42))[:5]
```

See [Choosing a Demeaner Backend](/how-to/demeaner-backends.qmd) for the
tradeoffs between MAP and `within`.

Use a seeded `np.random.Generator` for reproducible results. To inspect the
algorithmic Monte Carlo error, request diagnostics:

```{python}
diagnostics = fit.hatvalues(
    reps=200,
    rng=np.random.default_rng(42),
    diagnostics=True,
)
diagnostics.head()
```

`mc_low` and `mc_high` are pointwise Monte Carlo intervals for the numerical
approximation. They are not sampling confidence intervals for a population
quantity.

You can force `method="exact"` for a small multiway model to validate the
approximation. That path projects every column of the identity matrix and is
therefore unsuitable for large samples.

## Leave-one-out residuals

For OLS, the residual from deleting observation $i$ is

$$
e_{i,-i} = \frac{e_i}{1-h_i}.
$$

```{python}
loo = fit.loo_resid(
    reps=200,
    rng=np.random.default_rng(42),
    diagnostics=True,
)
loo.head()
```

An observation with leverage at or indistinguishably close to one cannot be
deleted while retaining an informative fit. PyFixest warns and returns `NaN`
when the estimated leverage or its Monte Carlo interval reaches that boundary.

## Generalized linear models

`hatvalues()` also works for `feglm()` and `fepois()`. It uses the weighted
projection from the final IRLS iteration, matching the conventional GLM hat
matrix and R `fixest` for nonlinear families.

```{python}
poisson_fit = pf.fepois("Y ~ X1 | f1 + f2", pf.get_data(model="Fepois"))
poisson_fit.hatvalues(reps=200, rng=np.random.default_rng(42))[:5]
```

`loo_resid()` is currently limited to OLS. In a nonlinear model, deleting an
observation changes the fitted means and IRLS weights, so the OLS identity above
does not produce an exact leave-one-out refit.

User-supplied regression weights and IV models are not supported in this first
implementation.
